items.plain: A farmer must plough, plant and water the field promptly, but has no power to make the crops sprout, flower and ripen on command; that happens in its own time as the seasons turn.
items.core_idea: Do your work, then let results come in time

items.plain: A divided community is one where mendicants quarrel and wound each other with cutting words; a harmonious one is where they live in agreement, valuing each other, blending like milk and water, and looking at each other kindly.
items.core_idea: Harmony means mutual kindness; division means wounding words

items.plain: A mendicant training the mind should balance three things: stillness, effort and calm detachment. Too much stillness brings laziness, too much effort brings restlessness, and detachment alone keeps the mind from settling deeply.
items.core_idea: Balance stillness, effort and equanimity in meditation

items.plain: Before awakening, the Buddha asked what attracts us to the world, what is wrong with it, and how to escape. Its pleasure attracts, its impermanence and suffering are the drawback, and letting go of desire is the escape.
items.core_idea: The world pleases, disappoints, and is escaped by letting go

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that three indulgences never satisfy: sleep, alcohol and sex.
items.core_idea: Sleep, drink and sex never truly satisfy

items.plain: When the mind is guarded, your actions in body, speech and thought are guarded too, and they do not rot; a person whose actions have not gone rotten will die well.
items.core_idea: A guarded mind keeps actions sound and death good

items.plain: Actions born of greed, hate and delusion are harmful, bring suffering and lead to more such actions. Actions born of contentment, love and understanding are good, bring happiness and lead to an end of action.
items.core_idea: Greed breeds harmful deeds; love and understanding breed good ones

items.plain: Three kinds of people rarely appear in the world: a fully awakened Buddha, someone who teaches what the Buddha taught, and a person who is truly grateful.
items.core_idea: Buddhas, true teachers and grateful people are rare

items.plain: Desire is bitterness, ill will is rot, and bad thoughts are the flies. If you are bitter and rotting inside, those flies will surely swarm and plague you.
items.core_idea: Desire and ill will draw bad thoughts like flies

items.plain: Some people are like a line carved in stone: they get angry often and their anger lasts a long time, the way such a line resists wind and water.
items.core_idea: Some people's anger lasts like a line in stone

items.plain: Some people are like a line drawn in water: even when someone speaks to them roughly and harshly, they stay in touch, keep dealing with them and greet them, and the offence vanishes at once.
items.core_idea: Some let harsh words vanish like a line in water

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to keep company with a friend who gives what is hard to give, does what is hard to do, and bears what is hard to bear.
items.core_idea: A true friend gives, does and endures the hard things

items.plain: Beings who do good in body, speech and mind in the morning have a good morning; at midday, a good midday; in the evening, a good evening.
items.core_idea: Doing good at any hour makes that hour good

items.plain: People will blame you if you lack learning and ethics, and praise you for whichever you have. If you both learn much and live ethically, they will praise you for both.
items.core_idea: Learning and ethics together earn full praise

items.plain: Craving goes with a person from life to life, and they never escape the round of rebirth. Seeing that craving causes suffering, a mendicant lets go of it and of grasping, and lives mindfully.
items.core_idea: Craving causes suffering and binds us to rebirth

items.plain: Whatever your posture, if you dwell on worldly thoughts, you have gone astray and cannot reach the highest awakening. A mendicant who has calmed their thoughts and loves peace of mind can reach it.
items.core_idea: Calm thoughts open the way to awakening

items.plain: There are four ways decisions get biased: by favouritism, hostility, foolishness and fear. If you act against what is right for these reasons, your good name fades like the waning moon.
items.core_idea: Biased decisions make your reputation wane

items.plain: Even at eighty or a hundred, if your speech is untimely, false and pointless, you are a childish elder. Even if you are young, if your speech is timely, true and useful, you are a wise elder.
items.core_idea: Wise speech, not age, makes someone a true elder

items.plain: If you are content with simple things that are blameless, cheap and easy to get, you will not fret about shelter, clothes, food or drink, and nothing will hold you back anywhere.
items.core_idea: Contentment with little frees you everywhere

items.plain: Discontent cannot overpower the attentive; attentive people are exactly those who overcome discontent.
items.core_idea: Attentiveness overcomes discontent

items.plain: You should live content, with a kind heart, mindful, your mind focused and calm within.
items.core_idea: Live content, kind, mindful and calm

items.plain: Someone who has goodwill, stays mindful, is calm within, and trains to let go of desire is called diligent.
items.core_idea: Goodwill, mindfulness and letting go make one diligent

items.plain: There are four ways of drawing people together: giving, kind words, caring for others, and treating people as equals. These hold the world together like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
items.core_idea: Giving, kindness, care and equality hold society together

items.plain: One way of deepening meditation is to know feelings, perceptions and thoughts as they arise, as they stay, and as they pass away; this leads to mindfulness and clear awareness.
items.core_idea: Watch feelings and thoughts arise, stay and pass

items.plain: The Buddha says you cannot reach the end of the world by travelling, yet there is no end of suffering without reaching it, because the world, its origin and its ending are found within this body and mind.
items.core_idea: The end of suffering lies within, not far away

items.plain: The sky is far from the earth and sunrise far from sunset, but farther still is the way of good people from the wicked. The company of the good stays steady; the company of the wicked is fickle.
items.core_idea: The good and the wicked are worlds apart

items.plain: When wife and husband are both faithful, generous, disciplined and living rightly, they speak kindly to each other, live at ease with their needs met, and their enemies lose heart.
items.core_idea: A couple equal in goodness lives in ease and kindness

items.plain: An old couple each tell the Buddha they have never betrayed each other even in thought and want to be together in the next life too. He says they should be equal in faith, ethics, generosity and wisdom.
items.core_idea: Lasting couples match in faith, ethics, generosity and wisdom

items.plain: When covetous greed, ill will, dullness, restlessness or doubt rules your heart, you do what you shouldn't and leave undone what you should, and your reputation and happiness crumble.
items.core_idea: A heart ruled by hindrances wrecks happiness

items.plain: One kind of happiness is being free of debt: a man who owes nothing, large or small, to anyone feels pleasure and happiness when he thinks of it.
items.core_idea: Owing nothing brings its own happiness

items.plain: Someone who knows the happiness of owing nothing, owning things and using wealth, and then looks wisely, sees that all of it is not worth a sixteenth of the happiness of blameless living.
items.core_idea: Blamelessness far outweighs the happiness of wealth

items.plain: Your parents are called Divinity, first teachers and elder gods, worthy of offerings. That is because parents do so much for their children: they raise them, nurture them and show them the world.
items.core_idea: Parents deserve reverence for raising and guiding us

items.plain: Those who judge by looks or are swayed by a voice are full of desire and do not understand. The fool, seeing neither what is inside nor outside, is carried away by a voice.
items.core_idea: Judging by looks and voices is foolish

items.plain: A wish for all living beings, every one of them: may they see only good things, and may no harm come to anyone.
items.core_idea: May all beings see only good and meet no harm

items.plain: When cattle cross a river, they all follow the bull, straight or astray. People are the same: when the leader behaves badly the whole country sleeps badly, and when the king is just the whole country sleeps at ease.
items.core_idea: As the leader goes, so go the people

items.plain: A new bride at first shows careful respect to her in-laws, husband and servants, but with familiarity she ends up telling them to go away. Mendicants slip the same way, so they should keep the heart of a new bride.
items.core_idea: Familiarity wears away early respect
items.extended_text: It’s like a bride on the day or night she’s first brought to her husband’s home. Right away she sets up a keen sense of conscience and prudence for her mother and father in law, her husband, and even the bondservants, workers, and staff. But after some time, because of living together and familiarity, she’ll even say to her mother and father in law, or to her husband: ‘Go away! What would you know?’ In the same way, on the day or night a mendicant first goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, right away they set up a keen sense of conscience and prudence for the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and even the monastery workers and novices. But after some time, because of living together and familiarity, they’ll even say to their tutor or mentor: ‘Go away! What would you know?’ So you should train like this: ‘We will live with hearts like that of a newly wedded bride.’

items.plain: The Buddha tells Potaliya that the finest person criticizes those who deserve criticism and praises those who deserve praise, truthfully and at the right time, because knowing the right time and context is best.
items.core_idea: Praise and criticize truthfully, at the right time

items.plain: A person who talks but does not act is like a cloud that thunders but brings no rain.
items.core_idea: Talk without action is thunder without rain

items.plain: A mendicant endures cold, heat, hunger, thirst, insects, weather, rude criticism, and even severe, life-threatening pain.
items.core_idea: Endure hardship, insult and pain patiently

items.plain: The Buddha names four kinds of things: unpleasant and harmful, unpleasant but beneficial, pleasant but harmful, and pleasant and beneficial.
items.core_idea: Pleasantness and benefit are separate questions

items.plain: A mendicant whose mind is no longer swayed by greed, hate, delusion or intoxication, having got rid of them, does not shake or grow nervous, and is not won over by other teachers' doctrines.
items.core_idea: A mind free of greed and hate stays unshaken

items.plain: Fear of guilt is when you think, 'If I did wrong in body, speech or mind, wouldn't I blame myself?' Afraid of that, you give up bad conduct, develop good conduct and keep yourself pure.
items.core_idea: Fear of self-blame keeps conduct pure

items.plain: A person can be in retreat in mind but not in body: they don't go off to the forest or wilderness, yet their thoughts are of letting go, goodwill and harmlessness.
items.core_idea: Retreat can happen in the mind, not just the place

items.plain: The Buddha names four kinds of brightness: the moon, the sun, fire and wisdom. The best of them is the brightness of wisdom.
items.core_idea: Wisdom is the brightest light

items.plain: The Buddha names four kinds of good speech: speech that is true, brings people together, is gentle, and is thoughtful.
items.core_idea: Good speech is true, harmonious, gentle and thoughtful

items.plain: There are two kinds of illness, mental and physical. Some beings stay free of physical illness for years, even a century, but almost no one is free of mental illness for an hour, except those who have ended the defilements.
items.core_idea: Almost no one is free of mental affliction

items.plain: The Buddha tells a nun her act was a foolish mistake, but since she has seen it and made amends, he accepts it. Recognising a mistake, dealing with it and resolving to restrain yourself is growth.
items.core_idea: Owning and correcting a mistake is growth

items.plain: The impatient way is to abuse, annoy or argue back when someone does that to you. The patient way is not to hit back when someone abuses, annoys or argues with you.
items.core_idea: Patience means not hitting back

items.plain: No one in the world, human or divine, can guarantee four things: that what ages won't age, what sickens won't sicken, what dies won't die, or that past bad deeds won't bear their painful fruit.
items.core_idea: No one can stop aging, sickness, death or karma

items.plain: The Buddha tells a brahmin not to speak of everything he has seen, heard, thought or known, nor of nothing. Speak of things that make good qualities grow and bad ones fade; don't speak of things that do the opposite.
items.core_idea: Speak only of what makes goodness grow

items.plain: People who fear death are those still craving sensual pleasures. When they fall gravely ill, they think the pleasures they love will leave them, and they grieve, wail and fall into confusion.
items.core_idea: Craving for pleasure makes us fear death

items.plain: The Buddha tells a mendicant that the mind leads the world and drags it around; whatever arises in the mind takes control.
items.core_idea: The mind leads and controls the world

items.plain: A truly wise person never intends harm to themselves, to others, or to both. When they think, they think only of what benefits themselves, others, both and the whole world.
items.core_idea: Wisdom means intending only benefit, never harm

items.plain: You learn a person's ethics by living with them, their honesty by dealing with them, their resilience in hard times, and their wisdom by talking with them, but only over time, with attention, and if you are wise.
items.core_idea: Character is known over long, attentive acquaintance

items.plain: Someone who loses family, wealth or health may reflect that this is how worldly life is: everyone meets gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. So they do not grieve and fall apart.
items.core_idea: Accept life's ups and downs without falling apart

items.plain: Good and true people encourage their followers to live free of greed, hate, delusion and aggression, so that they will not act from these in body, speech or mind.
items.core_idea: Live free of greed and hate to act well

items.plain: Queen Mallikā promises the Buddha that from now on she will not be irritable, even under heavy criticism, will give generously to spiritual seekers, and will not envy the possessions and honour others receive.
items.core_idea: Resolving to drop temper and envy and give

items.plain: The Buddha describes craving as a weaver that clings and creeps, choking the world and tangling it like yarn and matted reeds, so that it cannot escape bad rebirths and the round of rebirth.
items.core_idea: Craving tangles the world and traps it

items.plain: Hate can be born of fondness: when you love someone and others dislike them, you think, 'They dislike the person I like,' and hate for those others springs up.
items.core_idea: Love for one person can breed hate for others

items.plain: The Buddha names four things that greatly help a person: keeping company with good people, hearing the true teaching, thinking wisely, and practising in line with the teaching.
items.core_idea: Good company, true teaching, wise thought and practice help

items.plain: There are four ignoble searches: someone who will age, sicken, die and become corrupted searches only for things that also age, sicken, die and are corrupted.
items.core_idea: Mortal beings chase only what is also mortal

items.plain: Families lose their wealth because they don't look for what is lost, don't repair old things, eat and drink too much, or put an unethical person in charge. They keep it by doing the opposite.
items.core_idea: Wealth lasts through care, repair, moderation and honesty

items.plain: If a baby puts a stone in his mouth, a caring nurse will pull it out even if it draws blood and upsets him, out of kindness. Once the boy is grown and sensible, she stops worrying about him.
items.core_idea: Real care sometimes hurts, until the person can stand alone

items.plain: The Buddha tells Nāgita he wants no fame. Those who cannot easily enjoy the peace of renunciation, solitude and awakening as he does can have the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honour and popularity.
items.core_idea: The peace of renunciation beats fame and possessions

items.plain: As the spotless moon outshines all the stars, a person of faith and good ethics outshines all the stingy people of the world with their generosity.
items.core_idea: Generosity outshines stinginess like the moon outshines stars

items.plain: When you give, many people love and befriend you, your good name spreads, and a generous person can walk into any gathering confident.
items.core_idea: Generosity brings love, good name and confidence

items.plain: Good people, grateful and thankful, look after their parents, remembering what they did, and do for their parents what their parents once did for them.
items.core_idea: Care for parents as they cared for you

items.plain: Like a great banyan tree at a crossroads that shelters birds from all around, a person of faith becomes a refuge for many people.
items.core_idea: A person of faith shelters many, like a great tree

items.plain: A follower of the Buddha who wants happiness should not pray, hope or pine for it, but practise the way that leads to it; by practising it they gain happiness.
items.core_idea: Happiness comes from practice, not from wishing

items.plain: When someone close grows old, a wise disciple reflects that this happens to all beings, and that grieving would only harm their health, work and friends. So they don't grieve, and have drawn out sorrow's poisoned arrow.
items.core_idea: Everyone ages; grieving it only wounds you

items.plain: Grieving and lamenting does not do even a little good, and when your enemies see you are sad, they take heart.
items.core_idea: Grieving achieves nothing

items.plain: If chants, recitations, fine words or charity actually help, keep doing them. But if something good simply cannot be had, by you or anyone, accept it without grief: past deeds are powerful, and nothing more can be done.
items.core_idea: Accept what cannot be changed without grieving

items.plain: Everyone, lay or ordained, should often reflect: I will grow old, I will get sick, I will die, I will be parted from all I love, and I own my deeds and will inherit their results, good or bad.
items.core_idea: Reflect often on aging, sickness, death, loss and karma

items.plain: It isn't only me who must be parted from everyone and everything I love; all beings must be, as long as they keep being born and dying.
items.core_idea: Everyone must lose what they love

items.plain: The Buddha points to tree roots and empty huts and tells the mendicant to meditate, not to be negligent, so as not to regret it later. That is his instruction.
items.core_idea: Meditate now, so you won't regret it later

items.plain: A young mendicant reflects that old age will come and make practice in the forest hard, so they had better make the effort now to reach what they haven't yet reached, and so live at ease when old.
items.core_idea: Make your effort while you are young

items.plain: The lion strikes every prey with care, never carelessly, whether an elephant or a hare or a cat, so that he does not lose his way.
items.core_idea: Do even small things with full care

items.plain: A mendicant can live at ease in a community by keeping their own ethics without urging others to, watching themselves instead of others, and not being bothered by being unknown.
items.core_idea: Mind your own conduct, not others'

items.plain: A good carer can prepare medicine, knows what helps and what harms the patient, cares out of love rather than for gain, is not disgusted by bodily waste, and can encourage the patient with talk of the Dhamma.
items.core_idea: Good caregiving comes from skill and love

items.plain: The Buddha names five who sleep little at night: a woman longing for a man, a man longing for a woman, a thief longing for loot, a king busy with duties, and a mendicant longing for freedom.
items.core_idea: Longing and duty keep people awake

items.plain: A mendicant endures cold, heat, hunger, thirst, insects, weather, rude criticism, and even severe, life-threatening pain.
items.core_idea: Endure hardship, insult and pain patiently

items.plain: One kind of person gives someone robes, food, shelter or medicine, thinking, 'I give, this one receives,' and then looks down on the person they gave to.
items.core_idea: Giving can turn into contempt for the receiver

items.plain: A good person gives in five ways: out of faith, with care, at the right time, with no strings attached, and without harming themselves or others.
items.core_idea: Give with faith, care, timing, freedom and no harm

items.plain: There are five ways to get rid of resentment toward someone: develop love, compassion or equanimity for them, stop paying attention to them, or reflect that they own their deeds and will inherit the results.
items.core_idea: Love, compassion, equanimity or letting go dissolve resentment

items.plain: If someone's speech is bad but their actions are good, ignore their speech and focus on their actions, like a thirsty traveller who sweeps aside the moss on a pond to drink the clear water.
items.core_idea: Look past someone's faults to the good in them

items.plain: Sāriputta says that when accused, rightly or wrongly, gently or harshly, he will rely on truth and an even temper, saying plainly whether the fault is in him or not.
items.core_idea: Meet accusations with truth and an even temper

items.plain: You should not harm living beings, lie, steal, take others' partners or drink alcohol, which clouds the mind. Recollect the Buddha, reflect on the teaching, and develop a harmless, caring mind that leads to the heavens.
items.core_idea: Keep the precepts and cultivate a caring mind

items.plain: The Buddha says well-spoken words have five qualities: they are timely, true, gentle, beneficial and loving. Such speech is blameless and sensible people do not criticize it.
items.core_idea: Speak in time, truly, gently, helpfully and lovingly

items.plain: Tolerance has five benefits: most people like you, you are neither cruel nor full of regret, you die without confusion, and after death you are reborn in a heavenly realm.
items.core_idea: Tolerance brings goodwill, peace and a good rebirth

items.plain: Good conduct has five benefits: you don't blame yourself, sensible people praise you, you gain a good name, and you move away from false teachings and settle on true ones.
items.core_idea: Good conduct brings self-respect and a good name

items.plain: When you are joyful, rapture arises; rapture calms the body; a calm body feels bliss; and in bliss the mind becomes deeply still in meditation.
items.core_idea: Joy leads step by step to deep stillness

items.plain: Nakula's mother tells her dying husband not to die worrying, since worry is suffering. If he fears she cannot provide for the children and home, he need not: she can spin and card wool and will manage.
items.core_idea: Don't die worrying; those left behind will cope

items.plain: As night falls, a mendicant reflects that they could die tonight from a snakebite, a fall or an illness, and asks whether any bad qualities remain unabandoned that would stand in their way if they died.
items.core_idea: Ask each night what you would regret if you died

items.plain: A mendicant goes out, returns, stands, sits, lies down and works, all mindfully; practised this way, it leads to mindfulness and awareness of the situation.
items.core_idea: Do every daily act mindfully

items.plain: Being glad before giving, confident while giving and uplifted afterwards: that is the perfect offering.
items.core_idea: Give gladly before, during and after

items.plain: Greed does not lead to contentment, only to more greed. Hate does not lead to love, only to more hate. Delusion does not lead to understanding, only to more delusion.
items.core_idea: Greed, hate and delusion only breed more of themselves

items.plain: A white lotus grows in water but water does not cling to it. In the same way, the Buddha is born and lives in the world, but the world does not cling to him.
items.core_idea: Live in the world without the world clinging to you

items.plain: The Buddha tells Ānanda not to be judgmental or pass judgment on people, because those who judge others harm themselves.
items.core_idea: Judging others harms yourself

items.plain: As the moon's light outshines all the stars put together, diligence is the one quality that, when developed, secures benefits in this life and in lives to come.
items.core_idea: Diligence secures good in this life and the next

items.plain: When someone abuses, annoys or argues with an ascetic, the ascetic does not do the same back; that is how an ascetic keeps to their duty.
items.core_idea: A true ascetic doesn't retaliate

items.plain: The Buddha reminds Soṇa that a harp plays well only when its strings are neither too tight nor too loose. Likewise, too much energy brings restlessness and too little brings laziness, so Soṇa should find balance.
items.core_idea: Effort works best balanced, like a well-tuned string

items.plain: As wind cannot move a solid rock, sights, sounds, tastes, smells, touches and ideas, liked or disliked, do not disturb someone who is unaffected; their mind stays steady and free as they watch things pass.
items.core_idea: An unmoved mind is like a rock in the wind

items.plain: A calm mountain lake without a wave cannot be called forever still; a storm from any direction could stir it up again.
items.core_idea: Calm today does not guarantee calm forever

items.plain: Sensual pleasure is not the pretty things in the world but the greedy intention in a person. The pretty things stay as they are; the attentive remove their desire for them.
items.core_idea: Desire, not the world's beauty, is the problem

items.plain: The Buddha says that intention is what he calls action, because after choosing, one acts by body, speech and mind.
items.core_idea: Intention is what makes an action

items.plain: Birth, aging, illness and death are suffering; so are sorrow, grief, pain, sadness and distress, and not getting what you wish for.
items.core_idea: Life's losses and unmet wishes are suffering

items.plain: Overwhelmed by suffering, a person either grieves and falls into confusion, or searches outside for someone who knows a word or two that might end it. Suffering leads to confusion or a search.
items.core_idea: Suffering leads to confusion or a search for help

items.plain: A mendicant who loves company and groups cannot take pleasure in being alone in seclusion, and without that they cannot learn the patterns of the mind.
items.core_idea: Knowing your mind requires time alone

items.plain: The Buddha says you cannot reach perfection without giving up six things: conceit, feeling inferior, feeling superior, overrating yourself, stubbornness and grovelling.
items.core_idea: Perfection requires dropping conceit in all its forms

items.plain: A mendicant who enjoys the teaching, meditation, letting go, solitude, kindness and freedom from mental proliferation is full of joy here and now and has prepared the ground for ending the defilements.
items.core_idea: Joy comes from teaching, meditation, letting go and kindness

items.plain: Three bad qualities are discontent, cruelty and unprincipled conduct. To give them up, develop rejoicing, harmlessness and principled conduct.
items.core_idea: Rejoicing, harmlessness and principle replace their opposites

items.plain: Three bad qualities are discontent, lack of awareness and wanting too much. To give them up, develop contentment, awareness and having few wishes.
items.core_idea: Contentment, awareness and few wishes cure their opposites

items.plain: Three bad qualities are restlessness, lack of restraint and negligence. To give them up, develop calm, restraint and diligence.
items.core_idea: Calm, restraint and diligence cure restlessness and negligence

items.plain: The Buddha tells Ugga that fire, floods, rulers, thieves and heirs can take ordinary wealth, but not seven kinds: faith, ethics, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity and wisdom. Whoever has these is truly rich.
items.core_idea: Inner qualities are wealth no one can take

items.plain: A true friend gives and does what is hard, bears your harsh words, shares and keeps secrets, and never abandons you or looks down on you in trouble or loss. If you want a friend, keep company with such people.
items.core_idea: A true friend stays loyal through hardship

items.plain: Stay close to a friend with seven qualities, even if they push you away: they are liked and respected, they correct you and accept correction, they speak of deep things, and they don't urge you to do wrong.
items.core_idea: Keep friends who correct you and lead you right

items.plain: Nanda's mother tells of her only, dearly loved son being seized and executed by the rulers, yet she cannot recall becoming upset at any stage. The listener marvels that she keeps even her thoughts pure.
items.core_idea: Even in terrible loss, the mind can stay unshaken

items.plain: Arguments lead to lots of talking, talking makes people restless, restlessness loses restraint, and without restraint the mind is far from stillness.
items.core_idea: Arguments lead the mind away from stillness

items.plain: A mendicant who hears that nothing is worth clinging to comes to understand all things, watches every feeling as impermanent and lets it go, grasps at nothing, and so is free of anxiety and reaches nirvana.
items.core_idea: Grasp at nothing and anxiety ends

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants not to fear good deeds, because 'good deeds' is another word for happiness.
items.core_idea: Good deeds mean happiness; don't fear them

items.plain: An irritable person overwhelmed by anger is ugly, however well bathed, groomed and dressed in fine clothes they may be.
items.core_idea: Anger makes anyone ugly

items.plain: A person overwhelmed by anger takes what they don't need for what they need, and what they need for what they don't, and getting things so backwards brings them lasting harm and suffering.
items.core_idea: Anger makes you mistake harm for good

items.plain: An irritable person looks ugly and sleeps badly, mistakes what they need, may kill in word or deed, loses wealth and good name, and is avoided by family, friends and loved ones.
items.core_idea: Anger costs you sleep, wealth, name and loved ones

items.plain: Anger causes harm and disturbs the mind without the person seeing the danger. In anger you cannot see the good or the truth; you wreck easily what was hard to build, and afterwards you burn with remorse.
items.core_idea: Anger blinds you and destroys what you built

items.plain: Anger is a hidden snare of death in the heart. Cut it out with self-control, wisdom, energy and right views.
items.core_idea: Cut out anger with self-control and wisdom

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that all conditioned things are impermanent, unstable and unreliable, and that this alone is reason enough to grow disenchanted with them, let go of desire and be free.
items.core_idea: All conditions are unreliable, so let go of them

items.plain: Like a wise gatekeeper who keeps strangers out and lets friends in, a noble disciple guards the mind with mindfulness, giving up what is harmful and blameworthy, developing what is good, and keeping pure.
items.core_idea: Mindfulness guards the mind like a gatekeeper

items.plain: Thinking of your own good is reason enough to keep going diligently; so is thinking of others' good, or the good of both.
items.core_idea: Your good and others' good both justify diligence

items.plain: Human life is like a dewdrop on a blade of grass, gone as soon as the sun rises: brief, fleeting and full of suffering. So wake up, do good and live the spiritual life, for no one born escapes death.
items.core_idea: Life is a dewdrop; wake up and do good

items.plain: It is right to say today that human life is short, fleeting and full of suffering, so wake up, do good and live the spiritual life, since no one born escapes death. A long life now is about a century.
items.core_idea: Life is short; do good before death comes

items.plain: Loving even one creature with a heart free of hate makes you a good person; a noble one who feels for all creatures creates great merit.
items.core_idea: Love for even one being makes you good

items.plain: Do not kill or have others kill, do not conquer or urge others to conquer; with love for all beings you will have no enemy.
items.core_idea: Love for all beings leaves no enemies

items.plain: Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain are all impermanent. A wise, mindful person sees this, so the pleasant does not sway their mind and the unpleasant does not repel them.
items.core_idea: Life's ups and downs pass; stay unmoved by them

items.plain: It is good for a mendicant to look from time to time at their own failings and others', and at their own successes and others'.
items.core_idea: Review failings and successes, yours and others'

items.plain: The ocean floor slopes gradually with no sudden drop. In the same way, in the Buddha's teaching, awakening comes through gradual training and practice, not all at once.
items.core_idea: Awakening comes gradually, like a sloping shore

items.plain: As the ocean has only one taste, salt, the Buddha's teaching and training has only one taste, freedom.
items.core_idea: The whole teaching tastes of freedom

items.plain: Now that you have a human life and the true teaching has been so well taught, if you don't seize the moment you are wasting your time.
items.core_idea: Seize this rare chance; don't waste it

items.plain: A mendicant who has few wishes, contentment, solitude, energy, mindfulness, stillness or wisdom does not wish for others to know they have these qualities.
items.core_idea: True virtue doesn't seek recognition

items.plain: A good person is born into a family for the welfare and happiness of many: parents, children, partners, workers, friends, ancestors, rulers, gods and spiritual seekers, just as a great rain cloud nourishes all crops.
items.core_idea: A good person benefits everyone, like rain

items.plain: All the treasure in the world, pearls, gems and gold, is not worth a sixteenth part of a mind developed in love, just as starlight cannot rival the moon.
items.core_idea: A loving mind outweighs all treasure

items.plain: The Buddha tells Gotamī that whatever leads to passion, attachment, accumulating, more desire, discontent, crowding, laziness and being a burden is not his teaching; whatever leads to the opposite is.
items.core_idea: Test any teaching by where it leads

items.plain: Good friendship means spending time with people, young or old, who are mature in faith, ethics, generosity and wisdom, talking with them, and following their example.
items.core_idea: Befriend good people and follow their example

items.plain: Balanced finances means knowing your income and spending, being neither extravagant nor stingy, so that what comes in exceeds what goes out.
items.core_idea: Spend less than you earn, neither lavish nor stingy

items.plain: The Buddha tells a mendicant to train his mind to be steady and settled within, untouched by bad qualities. Then he should develop the heart's release through love, practising it fully until it becomes his foundation.
items.core_idea: Settle the mind, then build it on love

items.plain: The Buddha names eight noble ways of speaking: saying you haven't seen, heard, thought or known something when you haven't, and saying you have when you have.
items.core_idea: Say only what you truly saw, heard or knew

items.plain: As night falls, a mendicant reflects that they could die tonight from a snakebite, a fall, an illness or an attack, and asks whether any bad qualities remain unabandoned that would stand in their way if they died.
items.core_idea: Ask each night what you would regret if you died

items.plain: One ground for laziness: a mendicant has work to do and thinks it will tire the body, so they lie down instead of making the effort to attain what they have not yet attained.
items.core_idea: Avoiding tiredness becomes an excuse for laziness

items.plain: All things are rooted in desire and produced by attention. Contact is their origin, feeling where they meet, stillness their chief, mindfulness their ruler, wisdom their overseer, and freedom their core.
items.core_idea: Freedom is the core of all things

items.plain: One should see the body's unattractiveness to give up greed, develop love to give up hate, use breath meditation to quiet thinking, and see impermanence to uproot the sense of 'I am', reaching nirvana in this life.
items.core_idea: Specific practices uproot greed, hate and self-conceit

items.plain: Four things draw people together: giving, kind words, care and equality. The best gift is the teaching, the best kind words are teaching an eager listener, and the best care is helping others grow in faith, ethics, generosity and wisdom.
items.core_idea: The best giving and care is sharing the teaching

items.plain: The earth is not disgusted when clean and filthy things are thrown on it. In the same way, Sāriputta says, he lives with a heart like the earth: vast, limitless, and free of enmity and ill will.
items.core_idea: Keep a heart as accepting as the earth

items.plain: There are nine ways to get rid of resentment. One is to think, 'They harmed me, but what can I possibly do about it?'
items.core_idea: Letting go of what can't be undone ends resentment

items.plain: A foolish mountain cow, eager to try new pastures, lifts her back hoof before her front one is set down, so she never reaches the new place and never gets safely back to where she started.
items.core_idea: Rushing ahead without footing gets you nowhere

items.plain: Ānanda tells a nun of a meditative stillness that neither strains forward nor pulls back and isn't forced. Being free, it is stable; stable, it is content; content, one is not anxious. Its fruit is enlightenment.
items.core_idea: Unforced stillness is stable, content and free of anxiety

items.plain: A wild bull elephant who once lived crowded by the herd, eating trampled grass and drinking muddy water, now lives alone, free of all that, and happily scratches his itches with a branch.
items.core_idea: Solitude brings relief from crowded life

items.plain: Before his awakening the Buddha thought renunciation was good, yet his mind did not embrace it or find it peaceful. He realised it was because he had not seen the drawbacks of sensual pleasures or experienced the benefits of renunciation.
items.core_idea: Seeing pleasure's drawbacks makes renunciation feel peaceful

items.plain: Mean jealousy is given up not by body or speech but by seeing it clearly with wisdom again and again. It is wishing that someone else not prosper or not receive what they are given.
items.core_idea: Jealousy is overcome by repeated wise seeing

items.plain: Corrupt wishes are given up not by body or speech but by seeing them clearly with wisdom again and again. They are wanting to be known for faith, ethics, learning, solitude or energy that you do not have.
items.core_idea: Wanting credit for virtues you lack is corrupt

items.plain: King Pasenadi is said to be the greatest in his realm, yet even he decays and dies. Seeing this, a wise disciple loses their desire even for the highest, let alone for lesser things.
items.core_idea: Even the greatest decay, so desire fades

items.plain: A mendicant who wants to accuse someone should first check whether their own conduct is pure and blameless; if not, people will tell them to train their own behaviour first.
items.core_idea: Check your own conduct before accusing others
